newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel chief discounts inflation worries.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel chief discounts inflation worries.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Thursday that the weakening of the shekel over the past week would not necessarily lead to higher inflation.
"There are circumstances that exchange rate changes translate themselves relatively quickly to prices and there are circumstances under which this translation is not as quick," Frenkel told Reuters.
"It depends very much on the state of the economy, it depends very much on budgetary circumstances and it depends very much on monetary policy," he said.

The shekel has fallen sharply since last Friday, shortly after the government announced a reform of the exchange rate regime and the Bank of Israel lowered the base rate by a steep 1.2 percentage points to 12.7 percent.
In early trading on Thursday, the dollar was up 1.5 percent against the Israeli currency to about 3.58 shekels. Since last Friday, the dollar has gained about 4.7 percent against the shekel.
Israeli inflation has been slowing since April. But the economy has been slowing, too, and this year is expected to show its lowest rate of growth in seven years.

Frenkel, who was attending the annual general meeting of the Manufacturers Association trade group, said he did not believe the shekel would continue weakening. "I would not necessarily argue that a depreciation of a few days must continue with further depreciation," he said.
Nevertheless, he indicated that unlike most economists, the bank had not been surprised by the shekel's movement.

"Most commentators, politicians and others had fears of a strong appreciation of the currency. The Bank of Israel had argued that that's not a necessary presumption," Frenkel said. "As a matter of fact, there are good economic reasons for a depreciation."
Frenkel would not say whether the Bank of Israel would consider intervening in the forex market to stem a further depreciation.

"There are various assessments," he said. "We at the central bank will continue following very carefully the markets. I can assure you that no abrupt measures will be taken - the idea is steady as you go."
